A twin is one of two people or things that come from the same origin at the same time and are therefore closely linked as a pair. The word almost always points to one member of that pair — you use it to say that someone or something has a direct partner it came with.
Twins as People — The Most Common Meaning

When we talk about people, a twin is one of two children born to the same mother during the same pregnancy. So if your mother gave birth to you and your sibling on the same day, as part of the same pregnancy, then you are twins — and each of you is "a twin."

There are two kinds of human twins, and the difference between them is important:

Identical Twins

Identical twins begin life as a single fertilized egg (a single tiny cell formed when a sperm meets an egg). Very early on, that one egg splits into two, and each half grows into a separate baby. Because both babies came from the exact same original cell, they carry the exact same genetic information. This is why identical twins look so much alike — same face, same hair color, same eye color, same biological sex. They are, in a sense, nature's copies of each other. Scientists call them monozygotic twins (from one egg), but you simply call them identical twins in everyday life.

Even so, identical twins are never completely the same. Their fingerprints differ slightly, their personalities often differ, and life experiences shape them differently over time. They are extraordinarily similar, but they are still two distinct people.

Fraternal Twins

Fraternal twins come from two separate eggs, each fertilized by a different sperm cell — all within the same pregnancy. Because they started from two completely different cells, they share roughly the same amount of genetic material as any two ordinary siblings (about 50%). They just happen to have spent the same nine months in the womb and been born on the same day. Fraternal twins can look very similar or look nothing alike. They can even be of different sexes — one boy and one girl. Scientists call them dizygotic twins (from two eggs).

The key distinction to remember: identical twins look like each other because they share 100% of their DNA; fraternal twins may or may not look alike because they only share about 50%.
"A Twin" vs. "Twins" — How the Word Works in Grammar

This is a small but important detail.

"A twin" (singular) refers to one person from the pair.
→ "She is my twin." (= She and I were born together; I am talking about her as the one person who is my twin.)

"Twins" (plural) refers to both people together.
→ "They are twins." (= These two people form a twin pair.)

You would never say "she is my twins." One person is always a twin; the two of them together are twins.

Also worth knowing: twins are always specifically two. When a mother gives birth to three babies at once, they are called triplets, not twins. Four babies at once are quadruplets. The word "twin" strictly belongs to pairs of two.
Twins as Things — When the Word Applies Beyond People

"Twin" as a noun is not limited to people. It is used in several other contexts where the same idea applies: two things closely matched, paired, or produced together.

A counterpart or double: If one thing is called the twin of another, it means the two are so similar that they seem like they came from the same origin or are perfect matches for each other.
→ "This sculpture is the twin of one found in Rome." (= They are so alike they seem to be a matched pair.)

Twin cities: When two cities lie close together and are deeply connected economically or historically, they can be called "twins" or a "twin city." Each city is the twin of the other. Minneapolis and Saint Paul in the USA, for example, are famously known as the Twin Cities.

Twin bed: As a noun phrase, a "twin" or "twin bed" refers to a single-sized bed — typically used in the context of a hotel room or bedroom that has two separate single beds (one for each person). Each individual bed is a twin. A "twin room" is a room containing two such beds.

The Twin Towers: This is a well-known example of two structurally identical buildings being called twins. The original World Trade Center towers in New York City were called the Twin Towers because they were a matched pair — two buildings built alike, side by side.
A Rarer but Real Use — In Science

In the field of crystallography (the science of crystals), a "twin" or "crystal twin" is a single mineral specimen made up of two crystal structures that have grown together in a mirror-image or repeated arrangement. This is a highly specific scientific use, but it follows the same core idea: two matching things joined together.
The Thread That Runs Through Every Meaning

No matter how the word "twin" is used — whether for people, cities, beds, or crystals — the core idea is always the same:

One of two things that are paired together, usually because they came from the same source, were made at the same time, or are so deeply similar that they belong together as a matched set.

If you ever see the word "twin" used in a new context you haven't seen before, ask yourself: Is there a partner to this thing? Are these two things treated as a natural pair? If yes, then "twin" is being used correctly, and you already understand why.
